analysis.one_liner: Opens more federal land to oil, gas, coal, and mineral drilling and delays EPA air pollution rules.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy Committee in July 2013 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the government to offer large amounts of federal land for oil, gas, and coal leasing every year, speed up drilling permits, limit lawsuits over energy projects, and stop the EPA from finalizing several air pollution rules — including smog and tailpipe-emissions standards — until a new study of their costs was finished. It was referred to the Senate Energy Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies leasing federal land would gain the most: guaranteed annual lease sales covering at least a quarter of nominated acreage with no environmental review of the offering, drilling permits deemed approved after 60 days, bans on canceling sold leases or adding new lease conditions, and sharply limited court challenges including no attorney's fees for challengers. Refiners would benefit from a freeze on new clean-air rules; hard-rock mining companies from a new critical-minerals permitting and assessment program. Some renewable developers would get faster offshore wind test permits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil, gas, coal, and mining companies

how_it_helps.text: Title I would have created a committee to study the cumulative price impact of EPA fuel and refinery rules and barred the EPA from finalizing the Tier 3 vehicle-emissions rule and new ozone smog standards until at least 180 days after the committee's report [S2].

Titles II–IV would have required Interior to set production targets for federal land, offer at least 25% of nominated acreage at lease sales each year, deem drilling permits approved if the agency misses a 60-day deadline, and narrow court challenges to energy projects [S2][S3].
Title V would have mandated annual oil and gas lease sales in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska and set short deadlines for roads, pipelines, and permits there [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people near refineries, highways, and federal energy projects would bear the cost of delayed smog and vehicle-emissions standards and reduced ability to sue over federal energy projects, since attorney's fees and injunctions would be limited. Taxpayers would subsidize expanded leasing of public land, and the environmental review process protecting public lands would be narrowed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near polluting facilities and public lands

drawbacks.text: The bill would have barred the EPA from finalizing the Tier 3 vehicle standards and ozone smog standards until at least 180 days after a new interagency committee reported, and would have required cost and feasibility to be weighed in setting ozone standards, which public-health advocates would argue delays protections against smog and tailpipe pollution [S2][S3].

Judicial-review provisions would have limited lawsuits challenging federal energy projects: presuming agency findings correct, capping preliminary injunctions at 60 days, and eliminating attorney's fees under the Equal Access to Justice Act, making it much harder for citizens and conservation groups to contest projects on federal land [S3].

Mandatory lease sales would have required offering at least 25% of nominated federal acreage annually and shielded that acreage from environmental review, and an unapproved drilling permit would have been automatically deemed approved after 60 days [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered no meaningful benefit to ordinary people; its benefits flowed to energy companies through lower permitting friction, weaker environmental review, and delayed air rules, while its costs — more air pollution, fewer legal remedies for affected communities — fell on the public. It also died without ever being debated, so nothing changed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never acted on it, so the bill expired when the 113th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The Senate introduced S. 1401 on July 31, 2013 and referred it the same day to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee [S1][S5].
No further action appears in the bill's history: no hearings, no markup, no floor vote [S5].
The bill expired with the 113th Congress on January 3, 2015, having never received a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and coal interests are no better off, but neither are the public: the bill's streamlined permitting and review-rolling provisions never took effect, so environmental safeguards on federal land remained in place. The Obama administration's EPA rules were not delayed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: safeguards kept, nothing gained

for.name: Sen. John Hoeven
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its push to expand oil and gas production on federal land.

for.name: 10 Senate Republicans and Sen. Joe Manchin
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including one Democrat, Sen. Joe Manchin of West Virginia.

for.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors were Republicans except one Democrat, Joe Manchin; the bill never advanced far enough to produce a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill's core would have mandated lease sales on federal land, auto-approved drilling permits after 60 days, barred cancellation of sold lease parcels, and mandated annual leasing in the Alaska petroleum reserve [S2][S3]. Its cost is public land and air quality; its benefit is company revenue.

The bill would have blocked any new regulation of the 2008 stream buffer rule before the end of 2013 and set federal coal production targets, easing pressure on coal mining [S2]. Communities near mines bear the water and air consequences.
Refinery emission rules would have been frozen pending the new committee study, delaying compliance costs for refiners while residents near refineries wait longer for cleaner air [S3].

The bill would have created a critical-minerals permitting and assessment program, workforce grants, and repealed the National Critical Materials Act, speeding permitting for hard-rock mining [S2][S3].

Offshore wind test projects would have been exempt from environmental impact statements with 30-day permit deadlines, and wind/solar right-of-way fee revenue would fund agency processing [S2]. A genuine benefit, but modest in scope.
